parole.significato: The desiccated bodies of certain insects (female Kermes ilicis and Kermes vermilio), which live on the kermes oak, form…
parole.testo: From Middle French alkermès, probably from Spanish alquermes, from Arabic الْقِرْمِز (al-qirmiz), from Classical Persian کرمست (kirmist), from Middle Persian, from Sanskrit [Term?].

parole.significato: A heat stroke or fever, often suffered in the tropics.
parole.testo: From Middle French calenture, from Spanish calentura.

parole.significato: The upper robe worn by some bishops of the Anglican communion, usually without sleeves.
parole.testo: From Middle French chimarre, from Spanish zamarra. Cognate with French chamarre, simarre, Italian zimarra, of same origin. Doublet of simar, sable, and zimarra.

From earlier cumrade, camrade, comerade, camerade, camarade, from Middle French camarade, from Spanish camarada or Italian camerata (“chamber mate”), from Medieval Latin *camarata, from Latin camara, camera (“vaulted room, chamber”); see chamber. Compare camaraderie and chamberlain.

parole.significato: A hooped structure in cloth worn to extend the skirt of women's dresses; a hooped petticoat.
parole.testo: Hobson-Jobson of earlier forms vardingale, etc., borrowed from Middle French verdugale, from Spanish verdugado, from verdugo (“rod”).

parole.significato: A kind of open brimmed helmet used by footsoldiers in the 16th and 17th centuries, having no visor or bevor.
parole.testo: From Middle French morion, from, Spanish morrión, from morra (“upper part of the head”), from morro (“muzzle, snout”), from Vulgar Latin *murrum (“muzzle, snout”). Related to moraine (“an amassment of rocks on a glacier”).

parole.significato: A black person; a person of black African descent.
parole.testo: Alteration of earlier neger, from Middle French nègre (“a black person”), from Spanish negro. Ultimately from Latin niger (“black”), thus a doublet of negro and noir. parole.significato: A lowly person; a peasant or serf; a labourer who is obliged to do menial work.
parole.testo: From a combination of Middle French pion, peon and Spanish peón, both from Late Latin pedōnem (“pedestrian”). Doublet of pawn.

parole.significato: A light boat, traditionally propelled by sails, but sometimes a rowboat, and usually serving to carry messages among th…
parole.testo: From Middle French pinasse, from Spanish pinaza, from pino (“pine”) + -aza.

parole.significato: A slender, straight, sharply pointed sword (double-edged, single-edged or edgeless), designed predominantly for thrusti…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French rapiere, from Middle French (espee) rapiere, from Old French rapiere, raspiere, from Spanish raspadera (“poker; raker; scraper”), from Spanish raspar (“to scrape”), of Germanic origin. More at rasp.

parole.significato: Having a coat of a dark base color with individual white hairs mixed in.
parole.testo: From Middle French roan, probably from Spanish roano, from Old Spanish raudano, itself probably of Germanic origin (compare Gothic *𐍂𐌰𐌿𐌳𐌰𐌽 (*raudan), accusative of 𐍂𐌰𐌿𐌸𐍃 (rauþs, “red”). Compare rowan.

parole.significato: A type of light spherical combat helmet used in the 15th century.
parole.testo: From Middle French salade, from Spanish celada, thought to be from Latin caelāta (“ornamentally engraved [helmet]”) (although the Latin word is not attested in this sense).

parole.significato: A shark; now specifically, Sphyrna tiburo or Negaprion brevirostris.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French tiburon, from Spanish tiburón, of uncertain origin.
